clue.text: Preserve one's money here steal from library?

parts.note: to pocket something is to steal it
a book is what one takes from a library; the question mark flags the example

explanation.surface: An odd instruction to keep savings by pilfering from the public library.
explanation.definitionFit: A wallet or purse is the place where cash is kept safe, which is the sense here.

clue.text: Pole position

explanation.surface: A starting slot on the front row of a motor race.
explanation.definitionFit: A post is an upright stake of wood, and also a job or station held by someone.

clue.text: A cut in the work-force

parts.note: reads like a redundancy, but a short hairstyle shares its name with a ship's team, so this is both a haircut and a body of workers

explanation.surface: Job losses announced among the staff.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's company of workers is called by this word, which also names a very short haircut.

clue.text: Considering holding a party

explanation.surface: Thinking about whether to throw a party.
explanation.definitionFit: To give thought to an idea is to harbour it, and giving a party means hosting guests.

clue.text: Advocates running to build up beef, perhaps

indicators.note: in a down clue the pieces are stacked one above the next, building the word from the top

parts.note: barristers collectively are the Bar
something running is on, as a machine switched on

explanation.surface: Lawyers jogging to bulk up on red meat.
explanation.walkthrough: A baron of beef is a large joint of two sirloins, hence 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: A double sirloin joint is a classic cut of meat given this title.

clue.text: Our distant cousin failed to finish fruit, toyed with a nut

indicators.note: the fruit's word stops short of its final letter

parts.note: an orange is a citrus fruit

indicators.note: fiddling with the letters of the phrase rearranges them

explanation.surface: An ape abandons its orange and plays with a nut instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failed to finish' drops the E of ORANGE; 'toyed with' turns A NUT into UTAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Great apes are humanity's remote relatives in the primate family.

clue.text: Fanatical as a tanner of old

parts.note: a tanner was British slang for a sixpence, written 6d, that is VI (six) and D (old penny)

explanation.surface: Someone as zealous as an old-time leather worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tanner' looks like a leather worker; it is the old sixpence coin, written 6d in pre-1971 British money, with D the old penny.
explanation.definitionFit: Keen and eager to the point of obsession is the shared sense.

clue.text: Six men tease wily Oriental

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals

indicators.note: crafty or devious, so the letters of the following words are twisted

explanation.surface: Half a dozen men tease a cunning Easterner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wily' rearranges MEN TEASE into ETNAMESE, after VI.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from a country of South-East Asia is an Easterner by nationality.

clue.text: Lad gets up before end of debate to make revelation

indicators.note: the first piece comes ahead of the second
in a down clue going up means the letters are read bottom to top

parts.note: Sid, a typical boy's name, stands for a lad
a closure is the parliamentary motion ending a debate

explanation.surface: A boy rises before a debate ends to make an announcement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets up' turns SID into DIS, set before CLOSURE.
explanation.definitionFit: Making a fact known that was secret is an exposure or disclosed truth.

clue.text: Food is dear -must have money

parts.note: sweet and dear both mean lovable
bread is slang for money

explanation.surface: A complaint that groceries are expensive and need cash.
explanation.definitionFit: A pancreas or thymus gland eaten as a delicacy is a kind of offal.

clue.text: God, if he returned, would make a disaster of Eden

definitions.text: God, if he returned, would make a disaster of Eden

parts.words: God, if he returned, would make a disaster of Eden
parts.note: the king of the Greek gods, spelt backwards, names the canal whose 1956 crisis ruined Anthony Eden, the British prime minister

explanation.surface: A deity's second coming would wreck the Garden of Eden.
explanation.walkthrough: Eden is not the garden but Anthony Eden, the British prime minister brought down by the 1956 Suez crisis; the god's name backwards is SUEZ.
explanation.definitionFit: The ruler of Olympus in Greek myth is the deity meant.

clue.text: Children can be such magical creatures

explanation.surface: Kids may count as fairy folk.
explanation.definitionFit: Small ones are youngsters, and the phrase is also a name for elves and leprechauns.

clue.text: Our gangling daughter in disguise in dramatic entertainment

indicators.note: the letters wear a disguise, appearing in another order

explanation.surface: Our lanky girl dressed up for a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in disguise' rearranges OUR GANGLING plus D.
explanation.definitionFit: Paris's Grand Guignol theatre gave its name to gruesome melodramatic horror shows.

clue.text: Defenders gossip a lot out of turn

indicators.note: the letters are put out of their order

explanation.surface: People sticking up for someone chatter too much at the wrong time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of turn' rearranges GOSSIP A LOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who argue in favour of a cause are its champions in debate.

clue.text: Colour to flake off, causing litter perhaps

parts.note: orange is a colour
peel means come away in flakes

explanation.surface: Paint flaking off leaves a mess.
explanation.definitionFit: Discarded fruit skin is a typical example of rubbish dropped in the street.

clue.text: This way for the train

parts.note: reads like a station sign, but the railway track itself is called a way, lasting and fixed

explanation.surface: A signpost pointing passengers to the platform.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'permanent way' is the railway track and bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasting or fixed is the adjective, used in the railway term for the track on which trains run.

clue.text: Super with hired cap on

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece sits on top of the other

parts.note: to cap is to outdo or surpass
lent means let out for use, as something hired out

explanation.surface: A great hat, rented for the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cap' is not a hat but a verb, to outdo.
explanation.definitionFit: Super and first-rate are both terms of high praise.

clue.text: It's silly to wrap me in paper

indicators.note: the rearranged word goes round the next word, wrapping it
the letters are made silly, put in a foolish order

explanation.surface: Folly to gift-wrap oneself in newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'silly' turns IT'S into TIS; 'to wrap' puts ME inside: TI-ME-S.
explanation.definitionFit: The London daily newspaper of this name is the paper meant; it is also the paper printing this puzzle.

clue.text: Succession of Emperors, perhaps with new clothes

parts.note: a line is a dynasty, a series of rulers

explanation.surface: An allusion to the emperor's new clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the tale of the emperor's new clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Underwear and shirts were once collectively called by the name of the flax fabric.

clue.text: Edward's owner

parts.note: reads as whoever possesses Edward, but 'owner' means one who owns up, the title given to King Edward

explanation.surface: Whoever Edward belongs to.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward the Confessor was an English king before 1066; one who confesses owns up.
explanation.definitionFit: A priest hearing admissions, or one who admits sins, bore the epithet of the saintly English king.

clue.text: Leaves arm cover inside to air

indicators.note: the second word sits within the first

parts.note: greens are leafy vegetables
a sleeve covers an arm

explanation.surface: Instructions for hanging out a garment's sleeve to dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'air' looks like drying washing; it is a tune, the old English song.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous Tudor ballad tune is this song, and an air is a melody.

clue.text: Weep so much, almost making the place salty

indicators.note: the word is found within the phrase, not quite its whole length

explanation.surface: Crying so much the area becomes briny.
explanation.walkthrough: Epsom is a Surrey town famous for Epsom salts.
explanation.definitionFit: A Surrey town gives its name to the bath crystals called its salts.

clue.text: Dance by a single Indian

parts.note: a hop is an informal dance
I is one

explanation.surface: A Native American performing a solo dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pueblo people of Arizona are a North American tribe.

clue.text: Composer with hidden depths?

explanation.surface: A musician who is more profound than he looks.
explanation.walkthrough: Alban Berg was an Austrian composer; an iceberg hides most of its bulk below water.
explanation.definitionFit: The Austrian modernist Alban Berg is the musician; an iceberg mass hides most of itself under water.

clue.text: Eject the forerunner of Stevenson's blind beggar

indicators.note: the leading letter comes first, ahead of the rest

parts.note: Blind Pew is the sightless villain in Treasure Island by Robert Louis Stevenson

explanation.surface: Throw out the blind beggar's predecessor in a Stevenson novel.
explanation.definitionFit: To vomit or pour out forcefully is to throw something out.

clue.text: Call after schoolgirl trapped underground

indicators.note: the first piece comes after the second

parts.note: the Perse School for Girls is in Cambridge, so a Perse girl is a schoolgirl there
to phone is to call

explanation.surface: A phone call following a girl stuck in a mine or cave.
explanation.walkthrough: Persephone, in Greek myth, was carried off by Hades and kept in the underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek goddess abducted to the underworld spends part of each year confined below.

clue.text: Is he smoothly eloquent?

parts.note: smooth fabric is the material, and a QC, a senior barrister known for eloquent pleading, wears a gown of it

explanation.surface: A question about a smooth talker.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a Queen's Counsel 'takes silk' and is called a silk, after the gown.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior barrister, eloquent by trade, is named after the smooth fabric of his gown.

clue.text: Standing out as obvious about m-me, for example

definitions.text: Standing out as obvious about m-me, for example

indicators.note: the first word goes round the second

parts.note: staring, as in a glaring or stark error, means blatant
the printed letters with a stutter

explanation.surface: A speech defect is plain to hear in a halting 'm-me'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts MME inside STARING; the whole clue also describes the answer, of which 'm-me' is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking with halts and repeated sounds, as in 'm-me', is a stutter.
